pp:me:2016:q11.question: A single degree of freedom spring mass system with viscous damping has a spring constant of 10 kN/m. The system is excited by a sinusoidal force of amplitude 100 N. If the damping factor(ratio) is 0.25, the amplitude of steady state oscillation at resonance is ________mm.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Forcing function $=F_{0} \sin \omega t$

Given, $F_{0}=100 \mathrm{N}$

Damping factor,

$\xi=0.25$

Spring constant

$$\begin{aligned} k&=10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}=10 \times 1000=10000 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m} \\ A&=\frac{F_{0} / \mathrm{k}}{\sqrt{\left\{1-\left(\frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}}\right)^{2}\right\}^{2}+\left(2 \xi \frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}}\right)^{2}}} \end{aligned}$$

At resonance

$$\begin{aligned} \omega &=\omega_{n} \\ \therefore \quad A &=\frac{100}{10000}=\frac{0.01}{2 \xi}=0.02 \mathrm{m} \\ &=20 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}$$

pp:me:2016:q17.title: GATE ME 2016 | Set 1 | Question: 17
pp:me:2016:q17.question: Propane (C3H8) is burned in an oxygen atmosphere with 10% deficit oxygen with respect to the stoichiometric requirement. Assuming no hydrocarbons in the products, the volume percentage of CO in the products is __________

detailed_solution.markdown:
For stoichiometric burning (i.e., chemically correct),

number of moles of $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ required =5.

As it si burnt with 10 % deficient \mathrm{O}_{2} , it will generate CO.

That is, the new equation is

$\mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+0.9 \times 5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \alpha \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\beta \mathrm{CO}+\gamma \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

Balancing carbon atoms, we get

$3=\alpha+\beta \quad \cdots(i)$

Balancing hydrogen atoms, we get

$$\begin{aligned} 8&=2 \gamma\\ \text{or }\quad \gamma&=4\\ \end{aligned}$$

Balancing oxygen atoms, we get

$$\begin{aligned} 0.9 \times 10 &=2 \alpha+\beta+\gamma \\ 9 &=2 \alpha+\beta+4 \\ 5 &=2 \alpha+\beta\quad \cdots(ii) \end{aligned}$$

Eq. (ii) - Eq. (i), we get

$$\begin{aligned} 2&=\alpha\\ \text{or }\quad \alpha&=2 \end{aligned}$$

$\mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+\mathrm{aO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{bCO}_{2}+\mathrm{cH}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

Balancing carbon atoms, we get

$$\begin{aligned} 3&=b\\ \text{or } \quad b&=3\\ \end{aligned}$$

Balancing hydrogen atoms, we get

$$\begin{aligned} 8&=2 c\\ \text{or}\quad c&=4\\ \end{aligned}$$

Balancing oxygen atoms, we get

$$\begin{aligned} 2 a &=2 b+c \\ 2 a &=2 \times 3+4=10 \\ a &=5 \end{aligned}$$

Substituting $\alpha=2$ in Eq. (ii), we get

$$\begin{array}{l} \quad 5=2 \times 2 \times \beta \\ \text { or } \quad \beta=1 \\ \therefore \mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+4.5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{CO}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \end{array}$$

The volume percentage of CO in the product

$$\begin{array}{l} =\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}\right) \times 100 \\ =\left(\frac{1}{2+1+4}\right) \times 100 \\ =14.28 \% \end{array}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **14.3** (acceptable range: [13.7, 14.9]).

pp:me:2016:q21.title: GATE ME 2016 | Set 1 | Question: 21
pp:me:2016:q21.question: Under optimal conditions of the process the temperatures experienced by a copper work piece in fusion welding, brazing and soldering are such that

detailed_solution.markdown:
In welding, the two metals (or thermoplastic) must be similar. For example, copper cannot be welded to steel. Welding uses high temperatures to melt and join two metal parts. A filler metal is often used as well. When properly done, the finished weld is as strong as the surrounding metal.

Brazing joins two metals by heating and melting a filler (alloy) that bonds to the two pieces of metal and joins them. The filler obviously must have a melting temperature below that of the metal pieces. Brazing can join dissimilar metals such as aluminum, silver, copper, gold, and nickel.

Soldering  is a low-temperature analog to brazing. By the American Welding Society’s definition, soldering takes place with fillers (also known as solders) that melt at below $840^{\circ}F (450^{\circ}C)$. Metals that can be soldered include gold, silver, copper, brass, and iron. The filler, called solder, melts. When it solidifies, it is bonded to the metal parts and joins them. The bond is not as strong as brazed joint or welded one. Solder was once made mainly of lead, but environmental concerns are pushing industry to lead-free alternatives.

Therefore, the correct answer is **D**.

pp:me:2016:q29.title: GATE ME 2016 | Set 1 | Question: 29
pp:me:2016:q29.question:
Gauss-Seidel method is used to solve the following equations (as per the given order):

Assuming initial guess as $x_{1}=x_{2}=x_{3}=0$ , the value of $x_{3}$ after the first iteration is __________

detailed_solution.markdown:
We are given:

Initial guess: $x_1^{(0)} = 0, , x_2^{(0)} = 0, , x_3^{(0)} = 0$.

We rewrite the equations for Gauss-Seidel iteration:

From $x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 5$:

$x_1 = 5 - 2x_2 - 3x_3$

From $2x_1 + 3x_2 + x_3 = 1$:

$x_2 = \frac{1 - 2x_1 - x_3}{3}$

From $3x_1 + 2x_2 + x_3 = 3$:

$x_3 = 3 - 3x_1 - 2x_2$

First Iteration:

Step 1:

Compute $x_1^{(1)}$

Using $x_2^{(0)} = 0$, $x_3^{(0)} = 0$:

$x_1^{(1)} = 5 - 2(0) - 3(0) = 5$

Step 2: Compute $x_2^{(1)}$

Using $x_1^{(1)} = 5$, $x_3^{(0)} = 0$:

$x_2^{(1)} = \frac{1 - 2(5) - 0}{3} = \frac{1 - 10}{3} = \frac{-9}{3} = -3$

Step 3: Compute $x_3^{(1)}$

Using $x_1^{(1)} = 5$, $x_2^{(1)} = -3$:

$x_3^{(1)} = 3 - 3(5) - 2(-3) = 3 - 15 + 6 = -6$

Final Answer: After the first iteration, $x_3 = -6$.

Therefore, the correct answer is **-6**.

pp:me:2016:q37.title: GATE ME 2016 | Set 1 | Question: 37
pp:me:2016:q37.question:
A solid disc with radius a is connected to a spring at a point d above the center of the disc. The other end of the spring is fixed to the vertical wall. The disc is free to roll without slipping on the ground. The mass of the disc is M and the spring constant is K. The polar moment of inertia for the disc about its centre is $J=Ma^{2}/2$

The natural frequency of this system in rad/s is given by

detailed_solution.markdown: Total energy of system $$\begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} M v^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K x^{2}+\frac{1}{2} I \omega^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} M \times\left(a \times \frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K \times \\ \qquad \{(a+d) \theta\}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{M a^{2}}{2} \times\left(\frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}\\ \text{Let}\qquad \frac{d \theta}{d t}=\dot{\theta} \\ E=\frac{1}{2} M a^{2} \dot{\theta}^{2}+\frac{K}{2}(a+d)^{2} \cdot \theta^{2}+\frac{M a^{2}}{4} \dot{\theta}^{2} \end{array}$$ since energy of system remains concerned with respect to time. $$\begin{aligned} \frac{d E}{d t}&=0 \\ \frac{d E}{d t}&=\frac{M a^{2}}{2} 2 \cdot \dot{\theta} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+\frac{K}{2}(a+d)^{2} \\ & \qquad \cdot 2 \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}+\frac{M a^{2}}{4} \cdot 2 \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta} \end{aligned}$$ $0=M a^{2} \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{\lt a^{2}}{2} \cdot \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}$ Divide both sides by $\dot{\theta}$ $$\begin{aligned} 0&=M a^{2} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{M a^{2}}{2} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \cdot \theta \\ 0&=\left(M a^{2}+\frac{M a^{2}}{2}\right) \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \\ 0&=\frac{3}{2} M a^{2} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \end{aligned}$$ Divide both sides by $\frac{3}{2} m a^{2}$ $0=\ddot{\theta}+\frac{K(a+d)^{2}}{\frac{3 M a^{2}}{2}} \theta$ $\ddot{\theta}+\omega_{n}^{2} \theta=0$ Compairing above two equation $\omega_{n}^{2}=\frac{2 K(a+d)^{2}}{3 M a^{2}} ; \omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{2 K(a+d)^{2}}{3 M a^{2}}}$ Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

pp:me:2016:q38.title: GATE ME 2016 | Set 1 | Question: 38
pp:me:2016:q38.question: The principal stresses at a point inside a solid object are $\sigma _{1}=100$  Mpa, $\sigma _{2}=100$ MPa and $\sigma _{3}=0$ Mpa.  The yield strength of the material is 200 MPa. detailed_solution.concept: Strength of Materials - Stress-strain Relationship and Elastic Constants
detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{array}{l} \sigma_{1}=100 \mathrm{MPa}, \sigma_{2}=100 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{3}=0 \\ \sigma_{y}=200 \mathrm{MPa} \end{array}$$

According to Tresca theory

$$\begin{aligned} \tau_{\max } & \leq \frac{\sigma_{y}}{2 F O S} \\ \tau_{\max } &=\frac{\sigma_{y}}{2 n_{T}} \\ \text{now}\quad \tau_{\max _{\mathrm{abs}}} &=\frac{\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{3}}{2}=50 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \therefore \quad 50 &=\frac{200}{2 n_{T}}\\ \therefore \quad n_{T}&=2 \end{aligned}$$

According to Von-Mises theory

$$\begin{array}{l} \sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}-\sigma_{1} \sigma_{2} \leq\left(\frac{\sigma_{y}}{n_{V}}\right)^{2} \\ 100^{2}+100^{2}-100 \times 100 \leq\left(\frac{200}{n_{V}}\right)^{2} \\ \therefore \quad 100=\frac{200}{n_{v}}\\ \text{or}\quad n_{v}=2 \end{array}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

detailed_solution.markdown: $U_{0}=$ Velocity of free stream d= Boundary layer thickness at section c-d b= Width of the plate Velocity profile, $u=U_{0}\left[2\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)-\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)^{2}\right]$ Mass flow rate through section a-b, $$\begin{aligned} \dot{m}_{\mathrm{ab}} &=\rho A U_{0} \\ &=\rho b \delta U_{0} \end{aligned}$$ Mass flow rate through section c-d $\dot{m}_{c d}=\int_{0}^{\delta} \rho b d y U$ $$\begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{\delta} \rho b U_{0}\left[2 \frac{y}{\delta}-\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)^{2}\right] d y \\ m_{c d} &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\frac{2 y^{2}}{2 \delta}-\frac{y^{3}}{3 \delta^{2}}\right]_{0}^{\delta}\\ &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta}-\frac{\delta^{3}}{3 \delta^{2}}\right]\\ &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\delta-\frac{\delta}{3}\right] \\ &=\rho b U_{0} \times \frac{2}{3} \delta \\ &=\frac{2}{3} \rho b \delta U_{0}\\ \end{aligned}$$ Mass flow rate through section b-d, $$\begin{aligned} \dot{m_{bd}} &=\dot{m_{ad}}- \dot{m_{cd}} \\ &= \rho b\delta U_0-\frac{2}{3}\rho b\delta U_0\\ &= \frac{\rho b\delta U_0}{3}\\ \frac{\dot{m_{bd}}}{\dot{m_{ab}}}&=\frac{\rho b\delta U_0}{3 \times \rho b\delta U_0}=\frac{1}{3}=0.333 \end{aligned}$$ Therefore, the correct answer is **0.33** (acceptable range: [0.32, 0.34]).

pp:me:2016:q42.title: GATE ME 2016 | Set 1 | Question: 42

Taking $\log _{e}$ both sides, we get

$$\begin{aligned} \log _{e} 0.07143 &=\frac{-t}{16} \log _{e} e & &\left(\because \log _{e} e=1\right) \\ -2.639 &= \frac{-t}{16} \\ \text{or}\quad t &=42.23 \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$$
